{{Short description|Characterizes when a topological space is metrizable}}
In [[topology]], the '''Bing metrization theorem''', named after [[R. H. Bing]], characterizes when a [[topological space]] is [[metrizable]].

== Formal statement ==

The theorem states that a topological space <math>X</math> is metrizable [[if and only if]] it is [[Regular space|regular]] and '''[[Kolmogorov axiom|T<sub>0</sub>]]''' and has a {{nowrap|σ-discrete}} [[Basis (topology)|basis]]. A family of sets is called {{nowrap|σ-discrete}} when it is a [[union (set theory)|union]] of [[countably many]] discrete collections, where a family <math>\mathcal{F}</math> of subsets of a space <math>X</math> is called discrete, when every point of <math>X</math> has a [[neighborhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] that intersects at most one member of <math>\mathcal{F}.</math> 

== History ==

The theorem was [[mathematical proof|proven]] by [[RH Bing|Bing]] in 1951 and was an independent discovery with the [[Nagata–Smirnov metrization theorem]] that was proved independently by both [[Jun-iti Nagata|Nagata]] (1950) and Smirnov (1951). Both theorems are often merged in the Bing-Nagata-Smirnov metrization theorem. It is a common tool to prove other [[metrization theorem]]s, e.g. the Moore metrization theorem – a [[collectionwise normal]], [[Moore space (topology)|Moore space]] is metrizable – is a direct consequence.

== Comparison with other metrization theorems ==

Unlike the Urysohn's [[metrization theorem]] which provides a sufficient condition for metrization, this theorem provides both a necessary and sufficient condition for a space to be metrizable. Another theorem that provides both a necessary and sufficient condition for a space to be metrizable is [[Nagata–Smirnov metrization theorem]].
